Musical artist

**John Birks** "**Dizzy**" **Gillespie** ([/ɡ ɪ ˈ l ɛ s p i/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_ghih-LES-pee_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key");[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-3) October 21, 1917 – January 6, 1993) was an American [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz")[trumpeter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trumpet "Trumpet"), bandleader, composer, educator, and singer.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-obit-4) He was a trumpet [virtuoso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtuoso "Virtuoso") and [improviser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Improvisation "Improvisation"), building on the virtuosic style of [Roy Eldridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Eldridge "Roy Eldridge")[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-autobio-5) but adding layers of [harmonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmony "Harmony") and rhythmic complexity previously unheard in jazz. His combination of musicianship, showmanship, and wit made him a leading popularizer of early [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop") styles. His beret and horn-rimmed spectacles, [scat singing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scat_singing "Scat singing"), bent horn, pouched cheeks, and light-hearted personality have made him an enduring icon.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-obit-4)

In the 1940s, Gillespie, with [Charlie Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Parker "Charlie Parker"), became a major figure in the development of bebop and modern jazz.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-Palmer-6) He taught and influenced many other musicians, including trumpeters [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis"), [Jon Faddis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Faddis "Jon Faddis"), [Fats Navarro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fats_Navarro "Fats Navarro"), [Clifford Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_Brown "Clifford Brown"), [Arturo Sandoval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arturo_Sandoval "Arturo Sandoval"), [Lee Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Morgan "Lee Morgan"),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-jmh-7)[Chuck Mangione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Mangione "Chuck Mangione"),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-cm-8) and balladeer [Johnny Hartman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Hartman "Johnny Hartman").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-jmh2-9)

He won several [Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Awards "Grammy Awards").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-10) Critic [Scott Yanow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Yanow "Scott Yanow") wrote, "Dizzy Gillespie's contributions to jazz were huge. One of the greatest jazz trumpeters of all time, Gillespie was such a complex player that his contemporaries ended up being similar to those of Miles Davis and Fats Navarro instead, and it was not until Jon Faddis's emergence in the 1970s that Dizzy's style was successfully recreated [...] Gillespie is remembered, by both critics and fans alike, as one of the greatest jazz trumpeters of all time".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-AMG-11)

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dizzy_Gillespie&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

### Early life and career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dizzy_Gillespie&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early life and career")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/Dizzy_Gillespie_1955_Press_Photo.jpg/250px-Dizzy_Gillespie_1955_Press_Photo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dizzy_Gillespie_1955_Press_Photo.jpg)

Gillespie in a publicity photo (1955)

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e3/D._Gillespie%2C_J._Lewis%2C_C._Payne%2C_M._Davis%2C_R._Brown.jpg/250px-D._Gillespie%2C_J._Lewis%2C_C._Payne%2C_M._Davis%2C_R._Brown.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:D._Gillespie,_J._Lewis,_C._Payne,_M._Davis,_R._Brown.jpg)

Gillespie (_left_), with [John Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lewis_(pianist) "John Lewis (pianist)"), [Cecil Payne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Payne "Cecil Payne"), [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis"), and [Ray Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Brown_(musician) "Ray Brown (musician)"), between 1946 and 1948

The youngest of nine children of Lottie and James Gillespie, Dizzy Gillespie was born in [Cheraw, South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheraw,_South_Carolina "Cheraw, South Carolina").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-Africana-12) His father was a local bandleader,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-FinkelmanWintz2009-13) so instruments were made available to the children. James died when Dizzy was only ten years old.

Gillespie started to play the piano at age four;[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-14) by the time he was 12, he taught himself how to play the trombone and the trumpet.

From the night Gillespie heard his idol, [Roy Eldridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Eldridge "Roy Eldridge"), on the radio, he dreamed of becoming a jazz musician.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-Moody-15) He won a music scholarship to the [Laurinburg Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurinburg_Institute "Laurinburg Institute") in North Carolina, which he attended for two years before accompanying his family when they moved to Philadelphia in 1935.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-:1-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-17)

Gillespie's first professional job was with the [Frank Fairfax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Fairfax "Frank Fairfax") Orchestra in 1935, after which he joined the orchestras of [Edgar Hayes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgar_Hayes "Edgar Hayes") and later [Teddy Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teddy_Hill "Teddy Hill"), replacing [Frankie Newton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frankie_Newton "Frankie Newton") as second trumpet in May 1937. Teddy Hill's band was where Gillespie made his first recording, "[King Porter Stomp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Porter_Stomp "King Porter Stomp")". In August 1937, while gigging with Hayes in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."), Gillespie met a young dancer named Lorraine Willis who worked a Baltimore–Philadelphia–New York City circuit which included the [Apollo Theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_Theater "Apollo Theater"). Willis was not immediately friendly, but Gillespie was attracted anyway. The two married on May 9, 1940.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-:0-18)

Gillespie stayed with Teddy Hill's band for a year, then left and freelanced with other bands.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-jmh-7) In 1939, with the help of Willis, Gillespie joined [Cab Calloway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cab_Calloway "Cab Calloway")'s orchestra.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-:1-16) He recorded one of his earliest compositions, "Pickin' the Cabbage", with Calloway in 1940. After an altercation between the two, Calloway fired Gillespie in late 1941.

The incident is recounted by Gillespie and Calloway's band members [Milt Hinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milt_Hinton "Milt Hinton") and [Jonah Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Jones "Jonah Jones") in [Jean Bach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Bach "Jean Bach")'s 1997 film, _The Spitball Story_. Calloway disapproved of Gillespie's mischievous humor and his adventuresome approach to soloing. According to Jones, Calloway referred to it as "Chinese music". During rehearsal, someone in the band threw a spitball. Already in a foul mood, Calloway blamed Gillespie, who refused to take the blame. Gillespie stabbed Calloway in the leg with a knife; Calloway had minor cuts on the thigh and wrist. After the two were separated, Calloway fired Gillespie. A few days later, Gillespie tried to apologize to Calloway, but he was dismissed.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-19)

During his time in Calloway's band, Gillespie began writing [big band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_band "Big band") arrangements for [Woody Herman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woody_Herman "Woody Herman"), [Jimmy Dorsey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Dorsey "Jimmy Dorsey"), and others.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-jmh-7) He then freelanced with a few bands, most notably [Ella Fitzgerald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ella_Fitzgerald "Ella Fitzgerald")'s orchestra, composed of members of [Chick Webb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chick_Webb "Chick Webb")'s band.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-21)

Gillespie did not serve in [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). At his [Selective Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selective_Service_System "Selective Service System") interview, he told the local board, "in this stage of my life here in the United States whose foot has been in my ass?" and "So if you put me out there with a gun in my hand and tell me to shoot at the enemy, I'm liable to create a case of 'mistaken identity' of who I might shoot." He was classified [4-F](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selective_Service_System#Classifications "Selective Service System").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-Plummer-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-23)

In 1943, he joined the [Earl Hines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_Hines "Earl Hines") band. Composer [Gunther Schuller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunther_Schuller "Gunther Schuller") said,

> ... In 1943 I heard the great Earl Hines band which had [Bird](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Parker "Charlie Parker") in it and all those other great musicians. They were playing all the flatted fifth chords and all the modern harmonies and substitutions and Gillespie runs in the trumpet section work. Two years later I read that that was 'bop' and the beginning of modern jazz ... but the band never made recordings.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-Gourse2009-24)

Gillespie stated, "[p]eople talk about the Hines band being 'the incubator of bop' and the leading exponents of that music ended up in the Hines band. But people also have the erroneous impression that the music was new. It was not. The music evolved from what went before. It was the same basic music. The difference was in how you got from here to here to here ... naturally each age has got its own shit."[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-Dance-25)

Gillespie joined the big band of Hines's long-time collaborator, [Billy Eckstine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Eckstine "Billy Eckstine"), and it was as a member of Eckstine's band that he was reunited with fellow band member [Charlie Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Parker "Charlie Parker"). In 1944, Gillespie left Eckstine's band because he wanted to play with a small combo (which typically comprised no more than five musicians, playing trumpet, saxophone, piano, bass, and drums). Dizzy recommended [Fats Navarro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fats_Navarro "Fats Navarro") for the job with Eckstine, who proved to be an ample replacement.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-26)

### Rise of bebop

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dizzy_Gillespie&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Rise of bebop")]

[Bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop") was known as the first modern jazz style, but was unpopular at its onset. In fact, bebop was not considered revolutionary at first, but was seen as an outgrowth of [swing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swing_music "Swing music"). Regardless, swing introduced a diversity of new musicians in the bebop era, such as [Charlie Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Parker "Charlie Parker"), [Thelonious Monk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thelonious_Monk "Thelonious Monk"), [Bud Powell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bud_Powell "Bud Powell"), [Kenny Clarke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Clarke "Kenny Clarke"), [Oscar Pettiford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oscar_Pettiford "Oscar Pettiford"), and Gillespie. Through these musicians, a new vocabulary of musical phrases was created. Parker's system also held methods of adding chords to existing chord progressions and implying additional chords within the improvised lines. With Parker, Gillespie performed at famous jazz clubs including [Minton's Playhouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minton's_Playhouse "Minton's Playhouse") and [Monroe's Uptown House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clark_Monroe's_Uptown_House "Clark Monroe's Uptown House").

Gillespie compositions like "[Groovin' High](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groovin'_High "Groovin' High")", "[Woody 'n' You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woody_'n'_You "Woody 'n' You")", and "[Salt Peanuts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_Peanuts "Salt Peanuts")" sounded radically different, harmonically and rhythmically, from the swing popular at the time. "[A Night in Tunisia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Night_in_Tunisia "A Night in Tunisia")", written in 1942 while Dizzy was with Earl Hines's band, is noted for its syncopated bass line—a feature common in today's music.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-Vazquez-27) "Woody 'n' You" was recorded in a session led by [Coleman Hawkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coleman_Hawkins "Coleman Hawkins") with Gillespie as a featured [sideman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sideman "Sideman") on February 16, 1944 (on [Apollo Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_Records_(1944) "Apollo Records (1944)")), the first formal recording of bebop. Dizzy appeared in recordings by the Billy Eckstine band and started recording prolifically as a leader and sideman in early 1945. He was not content to let bebop sit in a niche of small groups in small clubs. A concert by one of his small groups in [New York's Town Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Town_Hall_(New_York_City) "The Town Hall (New York City)") on June 22, 1945, presented bebop to a broad audience; recordings of it were released in 2005. He began organizing big bands in late 1945.

In December 1945, Dizzy Gillespie and his Bebop Six, which included Parker, started an extended gig at [Billy Berg's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Berg's "Billy Berg's") club in Los Angeles. Reception was mixed and the band broke up. In February 1946, Gillespie signed a contract with [Bluebird Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bluebird_Records "Bluebird Records"), gaining the distribution power of [RCA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Records "RCA Records") for his music. He and his big band headlined the 1946 film _[Jivin' in Be-Bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jivin'\_in\_Be-Bop "Jivin' in Be-Bop")_.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-28)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8e/Dizzy_Gillespie_in_Helsingborg%2C_Sweden_1959.jpg/250px-Dizzy_Gillespie_in_Helsingborg%2C_Sweden_1959.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dizzy_Gillespie_in_Helsingborg,_Sweden_1959.jpg)

Gillespie performing in [Helsingborg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helsingborg "Helsingborg"), Sweden, 1959

Following his work with Parker, Gillespie led other small combos (including ones with [Milt Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milt_Jackson "Milt Jackson"), [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane"), [Lalo Schifrin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lalo_Schifrin "Lalo Schifrin"), [Ray Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Brown_(musician) "Ray Brown (musician)"), [Kenny Clarke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Clarke "Kenny Clarke"), [James Moody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Moody_(saxophonist) "James Moody (saxophonist)"), [J. J. Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._J._Johnson "J. J. Johnson"), and [Yusef Lateef](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yusef_Lateef "Yusef Lateef")) and put together his successful big bands starting in 1947. Gillespie and his big bands, with arrangements provided by [Tadd Dameron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tadd_Dameron "Tadd Dameron"), [Gil Fuller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gil_Fuller "Gil Fuller"), and [George Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Russell_(composer) "George Russell (composer)"), popularized bebop and made him a symbol of the new music.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-Yanow-29)

His big bands of the late 1940s also featured Cuban _[rumberos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuban\_rumba "Cuban rumba")_[Chano Pozo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chano_Pozo "Chano Pozo") and [Sabu Martinez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabu_Martinez "Sabu Martinez"), sparking interest in [Afro-Cuban jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afro-Cuban_jazz "Afro-Cuban jazz"). Gillespie appeared frequently as a soloist with [Norman Granz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Granz "Norman Granz")'s [Jazz at the Philharmonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_at_the_Philharmonic "Jazz at the Philharmonic").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-32)

Gillespie and his Bebop Orchestra was the featured star of the 4th [Cavalcade of Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalcade_of_Jazz "Cavalcade of Jazz") concert held at [Wrigley Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wrigley_Field_(Los_Angeles) "Wrigley Field (Los Angeles)") in Los Angeles, which was produced by [Leon Hefflin Sr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leon_Hefflin_Sr. "Leon Hefflin Sr.") on September 12, 1948.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-33) The young Gillespie had recently returned from Europe where his music was widely popular. The program description noted "the musicianship, inventive technique, and daring of this young man has created a new style, which can be defined as off the chord solo gymnastics." Also performing that day were [Frankie Laine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frankie_Laine "Frankie Laine"), [Little Miss Cornshucks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Miss_Cornshucks "Little Miss Cornshucks"), [The Sweethearts of Rhythm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Sweethearts_of_Rhythm "International Sweethearts of Rhythm"), [the Honeydrippers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Liggins "Joe Liggins"), [Big Joe Turner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Joe_Turner "Big Joe Turner"), [Jimmy Witherspoon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Witherspoon "Jimmy Witherspoon"), the Blenders, and the Sensations.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-34)

In 1948, Gillespie was involved in a traffic accident when the bicycle he was riding was bumped by an automobile. He was slightly injured and found he could no longer hit the B-flat above high C. He won the case, but the jury awarded him only $1,000 in view of his high earnings up to that point.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-Belli-35)

In 1951, Gillespie founded his record label, [Dee Gee Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dee_Gee_Records "Dee Gee Records"); it closed in 1953.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-36)

On January 6, 1953, he threw a party for his wife Lorraine at Snookie's, a club in Manhattan, where his trumpet's bell was accidentally bent upward. However, he liked the sound so much he had a special trumpet made with a 45-degree raised bell, a customization that would become his trademark.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-38)

In 1956, Gillespie organized a band to travel on a [State Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_State "United States Department of State") tour of the Middle East, which was well-received internationally and earned him the nickname "the Ambassador of Jazz".[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-40) During this time, he also continued to lead a big band that performed throughout the United States and featured musicians including [Pee Wee Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pee_Wee_Moore "Pee Wee Moore") and others. This band recorded [a live album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie_at_Newport "Dizzy Gillespie at Newport") at the 1957 [Newport Jazz Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport_Jazz_Festival "Newport Jazz Festival") that featured [Mary Lou Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Lou_Williams "Mary Lou Williams") as a guest artist on piano.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-41)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-42)

### Afro-Cuban jazz

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dizzy_Gillespie&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Afro-Cuban jazz")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a3/Dizzy_Gillespie_Giants_of_Jazz_1973_Dia0002.jpg/250px-Dizzy_Gillespie_Giants_of_Jazz_1973_Dia0002.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dizzy_Gillespie_Giants_of_Jazz_1973_Dia0002.jpg)

Gillespie performing at a [Giants of Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Giants_of_Jazz "The Giants of Jazz") concert in 1973 (behind him is drummer [Art Blakey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Blakey "Art Blakey"))

In the late 1940s, Gillespie was involved in the movement called [Afro-Cuban music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_of_African_heritage_in_Cuba "Music of African heritage in Cuba"), bringing [Afro-Latin American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afro%E2%80%93Latin_Americans "Afro–Latin Americans") music and elements to greater prominence in jazz and even pop music, particularly [salsa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salsa_music "Salsa music"). [Afro-Cuban jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afro-Cuban_jazz "Afro-Cuban jazz") is based on traditional Afro-Cuban rhythms. Gillespie was introduced to [Chano Pozo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chano_Pozo "Chano Pozo") in 1947 by [Mario Bauzá](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Bauz%C3%A1 "Mario Bauzá"), a Latin jazz trumpeter. Pozo became Gillespie's [conga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conga "Conga") drummer for his band. Gillespie also worked with Bauzá in New York jazz clubs on [52nd Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/52nd_Street_(Manhattan) "52nd Street (Manhattan)") and several famous dance clubs such as the [Palladium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palladium_(New_York_City) "Palladium (New York City)") and the [Apollo Theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_Theater "Apollo Theater") in [Harlem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlem "Harlem"). They played together in the Chick Webb band and the Cab Calloway band, where Gillespie and Bauza became lifelong friends. Gillespie helped develop and mature the Afro-Cuban jazz style. Afro-Cuban jazz was considered bebop-oriented, and some musicians classified it as a modern style. Afro-Cuban jazz was successful because it never decreased in popularity and it always attracted people to dance.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-ReferenceA-43)

Gillespie's most famous contributions to Afro-Cuban music are the songs "[Manteca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manteca_(song) "Manteca (song)")" and "[Tin Tin Deo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tin_Tin_Deo "Tin Tin Deo")" (both co-written with Chano Pozo); he was responsible for commissioning [George Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Russell_(composer) "George Russell (composer)")'s "Cubano Be, Cubano Bop", which featured Pozo. In 1977, Gillespie met [Arturo Sandoval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arturo_Sandoval "Arturo Sandoval") during a jazz cruise to Havana.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-44) Sandoval toured with Gillespie and defected in Rome in 1990 while touring with Gillespie and the United Nations Orchestra.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-45)

### Final years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dizzy_Gillespie&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Final years")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0d/Dizzy_Gillespie01.JPG/330px-Dizzy_Gillespie01.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dizzy_Gillespie01.JPG)

Gillespie in concert, [Deauville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deauville "Deauville"), Normandy, France, July 1991

In the 1980s, Gillespie led the United Nations Orchestra. For three years, [Flora Purim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flora_Purim "Flora Purim") toured with the orchestra. She credits Gillespie with improving her understanding of jazz.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-Jazzreview-46)

In 1982, he was sought out by [Motown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motown "Motown") musician [Stevie Wonder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stevie_Wonder "Stevie Wonder") to play his solo in Wonder's 1982 hit single "[Do I Do](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Do_I_Do "Do I Do")".

He starred in the film _[The Winter in Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Winter\_in\_Lisbon "The Winter in Lisbon")_ that was released as _El invierno en Lisboa_ in 1992 and re-released in 2004.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-Bivens-47) The soundtrack album, featuring him, was recorded in 1990 and released in 1991. The film is a [crime drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crime_film "Crime film") about a jazz pianist who falls for a dangerous woman while in Portugal with an American expatriate's jazz band.

In December 1991, during an engagement at Kimball's East in [Emeryville, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emeryville,_California "Emeryville, California"), he suffered a crisis from what turned out to be [pancreatic cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pancreatic_cancer "Pancreatic cancer"). He performed one more night but cancelled the rest of the tour for medical reasons, ending his 56-year touring career. He led his last recording session on January 25, 1992.

Gillespie and his touring band performed at Jazz Alley in [Seattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle "Seattle") for several successive days, the final performance of his touring career being February 29, 1992.

On November 26, 1992, [Carnegie Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Hall "Carnegie Hall"), following the Second [Baháʼí World Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bah%C3%A1%CA%BC%C3%AD_World_Congress "Baháʼí World Congress"), celebrated Gillespie's 75th birthday concert and his offering to the celebration of the centenary of the passing of [Baháʼu'lláh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bah%C3%A1%CA%BCu'll%C3%A1h "Baháʼu'lláh"). Gillespie was to appear at Carnegie Hall for the 33rd time. The line-up included [Jon Faddis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Faddis "Jon Faddis"), [James Moody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Moody_(saxophonist) "James Moody (saxophonist)"), [Paquito D'Rivera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paquito_D'Rivera "Paquito D'Rivera"), and the [Mike Longo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Longo "Mike Longo") Trio with [Ben Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Brown_(musician) "Ben Brown (musician)") on bass and [Mickey Roker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mickey_Roker "Mickey Roker") on drums. Gillespie was too unwell to attend, "But the musicians played their real hearts out for him, no doubt suspecting that he would not play again. Each musician gave tribute to their friend, this great soul and innovator in the world of jazz."[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-Johnson-48)

### Death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dizzy_Gillespie&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Death")]

A longtime resident of [Englewood, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Englewood,_New_Jersey "Englewood, New Jersey"),[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-Berman-49) Gillespie died of [pancreatic cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pancreatic_cancer "Pancreatic cancer") on January 6, 1993, at the age of 75.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-50) His funeral was held on January 12 at St. Peter's Lutheran Church, with [Roberta Flack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberta_Flack "Roberta Flack") singing "[Amazing Grace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazing_Grace "Amazing Grace")".[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-53) His grave in [Flushing Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flushing_Cemetery "Flushing Cemetery"), Queens, is unmarked.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-54)

## Politics and religion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dizzy_Gillespie&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Politics and religion")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/46/Dizzy_for_President_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Dizzy_for_President_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dizzy_for_President_(cropped).jpg)

A "Dizzy Gillespie for President" pinback button, 1964

In 1962, Gillespie and actor [George Mathews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Mathews_(actor) "George Mathews (actor)") starred in _[The Hole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Hole\_(1962\_film) "The Hole (1962 film)")_, an animated short film by [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hubley "John Hubley") and [Faith Hubley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Hubley "Faith Hubley"). Released the same year as the [Cuban Missile Crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuban_Missile_Crisis "Cuban Missile Crisis"), it uses audio from an improvised conversation between the two debating the causes of accidents and the possibility of accidentally launching [nuclear weapons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapon "Nuclear weapon"). The short went on to win the [Academy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards") for [Best Animated Short Film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Animated_Short_Film "Academy Award for Best Animated Short Film") the following year.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-55)

During the [1964 United States presidential campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_United_States_presidential_election "1964 United States presidential election"), Gillespie put himself forward as an independent [write-in candidate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Write-in_candidate "Write-in candidate").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-Gillespie-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-Lipsitz-57) He promised that if he were elected, the [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House") would be renamed the Blues House, and he would have a cabinet composed of [Duke Ellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Ellington "Duke Ellington") (Secretary of State), [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis") (Director of the CIA), [Max Roach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Roach "Max Roach") (Secretary of Defense), [Charles Mingus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus "Charles Mingus") (Secretary of Peace), [Ray Charles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Charles "Ray Charles") (Librarian of Congress), [Louis Armstrong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Armstrong "Louis Armstrong") (Secretary of Agriculture), [Mary Lou Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Lou_Williams "Mary Lou Williams") (Ambassador to the Vatican), [Thelonious Monk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thelonious_Monk "Thelonious Monk") (Travelling Ambassador), and [Malcolm X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malcolm_X "Malcolm X") (Attorney General).[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-Prez-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-59) He said his running mate would be [Phyllis Diller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phyllis_Diller "Phyllis Diller"). Campaign buttons had been manufactured years before by Gillespie's booking agency as a joke,[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-60) but proceeds went to the [Congress of Racial Equality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congress_of_Racial_Equality "Congress of Racial Equality"), the [Southern Christian Leadership Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Christian_Leadership_Conference "Southern Christian Leadership Conference"), and [Martin Luther King Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr. "Martin Luther King Jr.");[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-61) in later years they became a collector's item.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-62) In 1971, he announced he would run again[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-64) but withdrew before the [election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_United_States_presidential_election "1972 United States presidential election").[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-65)

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8f/Dizzy_Gillespie_holding_memoir_%22To_Be_or_Not_to_Bop%22.jpg/250px-Dizzy_Gillespie_holding_memoir_%22To_Be_or_Not_to_Bop%22.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dizzy_Gillespie_holding_memoir_%22To_Be_or_Not_to_Bop%22.jpg)

Gillespie holding his memoir: _[To Be or Not to Bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/To\_Be\_or\_Not\_to\_Bop "To Be or Not to Bop")_ (1979)

Shortly after the death of [Charlie Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Parker "Charlie Parker"), Gillespie encountered an audience member after a show. They had a conversation about the oneness of humanity and the elimination of racism from the perspective of the [Baháʼí Faith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bah%C3%A1%CA%BC%C3%AD_Faith "Baháʼí Faith"). Impacted by the [assassination of Martin Luther King Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Martin_Luther_King_Jr. "Assassination of Martin Luther King Jr.") in 1968, he became a Baháʼí that same year.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-Gillespie2009-66)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-Hearing-67) The universalist emphasis of his religion prodded him to see himself more as a global citizen and humanitarian, expanding on his interest in his African heritage. His spirituality brought out generosity and what author [Nat Hentoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nat_Hentoff "Nat Hentoff") called an inner strength, discipline, and "soul force".[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-Shipton-68)

Gillespie's conversion was most affected by [Bill Sears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Sears_(Bah%C3%A1%CA%BC%C3%AD) "William Sears (Baháʼí)")' book _Thief in the Night_.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-Gillespie2009-66) Gillespie spoke about the Baháʼí Faith frequently on his trips abroad.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-69)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-bahai1-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-Pokorny-71) He is honored with weekly jazz sessions at the New York Baháʼí Center in the memorial auditorium.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-72) A concert in honor of his 75th birthday was held in New York City's [Carnegie Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Hall "Carnegie Hall"), November 26, 1992, in conjunction with the [second Baháʼí World Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bah%C3%A1%CA%BC%C3%AD_World_Congress#1992:_Second_Bah%C3%A1%CA%BC%C3%AD_World_Congress "Baháʼí World Congress"), however, he was too ill to personally attend.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-73)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-75)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dizzy_Gillespie&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Gillespie married dancer Lorraine Willis in [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston") on May 9, 1940.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-:1-16) They remained together until his death in 1993; Lorraine converted to Catholicism with [Mary Lou Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Lou_Williams "Mary Lou Williams") in 1957.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-:0-18)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-76) Lorraine managed his business and personal affairs.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-77) The couple had no children, but Gillespie fathered a daughter, jazz singer [Jeanie Bryson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeanie_Bryson "Jeanie Bryson"), born in 1958 from an affair with songwriter Connie Bryson.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-78)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-:2-79) Gillespie met Bryson, a [Juilliard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juilliard_School "Juilliard School")-trained pianist, at the [Birdland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birdland_(New_York_jazz_club) "Birdland (New York jazz club)") jazz club in New York City.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-:2-79) In the mid-1960s, Gillespie settled down in [Englewood, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Englewood,_New_Jersey "Englewood, New Jersey"), with his wife.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-80) The local Englewood public high school, [Dwight Morrow High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dwight_Morrow_High_School "Dwight Morrow High School"), named its auditorium after him: the Dizzy Gillespie Auditorium.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-81)[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-82)

## Artistry

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dizzy_Gillespie&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Artistry")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/48/Dizzy_Gillespie-140912-0009-98WP.jpg/330px-Dizzy_Gillespie-140912-0009-98WP.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dizzy_Gillespie-140912-0009-98WP.jpg)

Gillespie performing for [The Giants of Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Giants_of_Jazz "The Giants of Jazz") in 1971, an exemplar shown also of his cheek-oriented [laryngoceles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laryngocele "Laryngocele")

### Style

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dizzy_Gillespie&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Style")]

Gillespie has been described as the "sound of surprise".[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-Shipton-68)_The Rough Guide to Jazz_ describes his musical style:

> The whole essence of a Gillespie solo was cliff-hanging suspense: the phrases and the angle of the approach were perpetually varied, breakneck runs were followed by pauses, by huge interval leaps, by long, immensely high notes, by slurs and smears and bluesy phrases; he always took listeners by surprise, always shocking them with a new thought. His lightning reflexes and superb ear meant his instrumental execution matched his thoughts in its power and speed. And he was concerned at all times with swing—even taking the most daring liberties with pulse or beat, his phrases never failed to swing. Gillespie's magnificent sense of time and emotional intensity of his playing came from childhood roots. His parents were Methodists, but as a boy he used to sneak off every Sunday to the uninhibited Sanctified Church. He said later, "The Sanctified Church had deep significance for me musically. I first learned the significance of rhythm there and all about how music can transport people spiritually."[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-rough-83)

In Gillespie's obituary, Peter Watrous describes his performance style:

> In the naturally effervescent Mr. Gillespie, opposites existed. His playing—and he performed constantly until nearly the end of his life—was meteoric, full of virtuosic invention and deadly serious. But with his endlessly funny asides, his huge variety of facial expressions and his natural comic gifts, he was as much a pure entertainer as an accomplished artist.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-obit-4)

[Wynton Marsalis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wynton_Marsalis "Wynton Marsalis") summarized Gillespie as a player and teacher:

> His playing showcases the importance of intelligence. His rhythmic sophistication was unequaled. He was a master of harmony—and fascinated with studying it. He took in all the music of his youth—from Roy Eldridge to Duke Ellington—and developed a unique style built on complex rhythm and harmony balanced by wit. Gillespie was so quick-minded, he could create an endless flow of ideas at unusually fast tempo. Nobody had ever even considered playing a trumpet that way, let alone had actually tried. All the musicians respected him because, in addition to outplaying everyone, he knew so much and was so generous with that knowledge...[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-Marsalis-84)

### Bent trumpet

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dizzy_Gillespie&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Bent trumpet")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/31/DIG15178-014_%2853537432815%29.jpg/330px-DIG15178-014_%2853537432815%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:DIG15178-014_(53537432815).jpg)

Gillespie's bent trumpet on display at the [LBJ Presidential Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyndon_Baines_Johnson_Library_and_Museum "Lyndon Baines Johnson Library and Museum") in February 2024

Gillespie's trademark trumpet featured a bell which bent upward at a 45-degree angle rather than pointing straight ahead as in the conventional design. According to Gillespie's autobiography, this was originally the result of accidental damage caused by the dancers [Stump and Stumpy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stump_and_Stumpy "Stump and Stumpy") falling onto the instrument while it was on a trumpet stand on stage at Snookie's in Manhattan on January 6, 1953, during a birthday party for Gillespie's wife Lorraine.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-85) The constriction caused by the bending altered the tone of the instrument, and Gillespie liked the effect. He had the trumpet straightened out the next day, but he could not forget the tone. Gillespie sent a request to the [Martin Band Instrument Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Band_Instrument_Company "Martin Band Instrument Company") to make him a "bent" trumpet from a sketch produced by Lorraine, and from that time forward played a trumpet with an upturned bell.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-Hamlin-86)

By June 1954, he was using a professionally manufactured horn of this design, and it was to become a trademark for the rest of his life.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-Shipton-68):258–259 Such trumpets were made for him by Martin (from 1954), [King Musical Instruments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Musical_Instruments "King Musical Instruments") (from 1972), and [Renold Schilke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renold_Schilke "Renold Schilke") (from 1982, a gift from [Jon Faddis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Faddis "Jon Faddis")).[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-Hamlin-86) Gillespie favored mouthpieces made by [Al Cass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Cass "Al Cass"). In December 1986, Gillespie gifted the [National Museum of American History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History "National Museum of American History") his 1972 King "Silver Flair" trumpet with a Cass mouthpiece.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-Hamlin-86)[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-NMAH-87)

In April 1995, Gillespie's Martin trumpet was auctioned at [Christie's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christie's "Christie's") in New York City alongside instruments used by [Coleman Hawkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coleman_Hawkins "Coleman Hawkins"), [Jimi Hendrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimi_Hendrix "Jimi Hendrix"), and [Elvis Presley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elvis_Presley "Elvis Presley").[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-88) An image of Gillespie's trumpet was selected for the cover of the auction program. The battered instrument was sold to Manhattan builder Jeffery Brown for $63,000, the proceeds benefiting jazz musicians with cancer.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-89)[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-90)[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-91)

## Awards and honors

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dizzy_Gillespie&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Awards and honors")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e4/Dizzy_Gillespie_statue.jpg/250px-Dizzy_Gillespie_statue.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dizzy_Gillespie_statue.jpg)

Statue of Gillespie, by Ed Dwight, in his hometown of [Cheraw, South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheraw,_South_Carolina "Cheraw, South Carolina")

In 1989, Gillespie received the [Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Lifetime_Achievement_Award "Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award"). The next year, at the [Kennedy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Center "Kennedy Center") ceremonies celebrating the centennial of American jazz, Gillespie was awarded the [Kennedy Center Honors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Center_Honors "Kennedy Center Honors") and the [American Society of Composers, Authors, and Publishers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Society_of_Composers,_Authors_and_Publishers "American Society of Composers, Authors and Publishers") (ASCAP) _Duke Ellington Award_ for 50 years of achievement as a composer, performer, and bandleader.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-tribute-92)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-93)

In 1989, Gillespie was awarded with an honorary doctorate of music from [Berklee College of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berklee_College_of_Music "Berklee College of Music").[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-94)

In 1991, Gillespie received the Golden Plate Award of the [American Academy of Achievement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Academy_of_Achievement "American Academy of Achievement"), presented by Awards Council member [Wynton Marsalis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wynton_Marsalis "Wynton Marsalis").[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-95)

In 1993, he received the [Polar Music Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polar_Music_Prize "Polar Music Prize") in Sweden.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-polar-96) In 2002, he was posthumously inducted into the [International Latin Music Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Latin_Music_Hall_of_Fame "International Latin Music Hall of Fame") for his contributions to Afro-Cuban music.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-97) He was honored on December 31, 2006, in "A Jazz New Year's Eve: Freddy Cole & the Dizzy Gillespie All-Star Big Band" at the Kennedy Center.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-98) In 2014, Gillespie was inducted into the [New Jersey Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey_Hall_of_Fame "New Jersey Hall of Fame").[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie#cite_note-99)

# “Dizzier and Dizzier” (1949) Dizzy Gillespie/Gerald Wilson / (1968) Frankie Carle/Lew Quadling with Conte Candoli and Georgie Auld

![Image 1](https://swingandbeyond.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/DG-Complete-Victor-649x400.jpg)

[Video 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Fj-CWWX6Nso)

## **“Dizzier and Dizzier”**

(aka “Katy”)

Composed and arranged by Gerald Wilson.

**Recorded by Dizzy Gillespie and His Orchestra for RCA Victor on May 6, 1949 in Chicago.**

John B. “Dizzy” Gillespie, trumpet, directing: Benny Harris and Elmon Wright and Willie Cook, trumpets; Andy Duryea, Sam Hurt, Jesse Tarrant, trombones; John Brown and Ernie Henry, alto saxophones; Yusef Lateef and Joe Gayles, tenor saxophones; Al Gibson, baritone saxophone; James “Hen Gates” Foreman, piano; Al McKibbon, bass; Teddy Stewart, drums.

**The story:**

**John Birks “Dizzy” Gillespie** (1917-1993), the youngest of nine children of Lottie and James Gillespie, was born in Cheraw, South Carolina. His father was a local bandleader, so instruments were made available to the Gillespie children, including John. James died when John was only ten years old.

John Gillespie started to play the piano at age four; and by the time he was 12, he had taught himself how to play the trombone and the trumpet.

From the night in the mid-1930s Gillespie when heard trumpet wizard Roy Eldridge on the radio, he dreamed of becoming a professional musician. He won a music scholarship to the Laurinburg Institute in North Carolina, where he attended for two years, from age sixteen to eighteen. During this time, he studied harmony and theory, but not trumpet. Nevertheless, he continued developing proficiency on that instrument. He moved with his family to Philadelphia in 1935.

![Image 2](https://swingandbeyond.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Dizzy-1930s-2.jpg)Gillespie’s first job as a professional trumpeter was with Frank Fairfax’s band in 1935. Another young trumpeter was in that band then, Charlie Shavers. Gillespie, Shavers, and a bit later, Harry Edison were young musicians who advanced the technical possibilities of the trumpet in the late 1930s and into the 1940s. Stylistically, Gillespie was a follower of Roy Eldridge in the mid and late 1930s. He replaced Frankie Newton (who had previously replaced Roy Eldridge) (1) in Teddy Hill’s band in May of 1937, then he went on tour of France and England in the summer of 1937 with the Hill band. _(A link to a recording Gillespie made with Teddy Hill can be accessed at endnote 2.)_

Gillespie earned his nickname “Dizzy” while playing with the Fairfax band. It was bestowed upon him by colleagues because of his clowning, which happened both onstage and off. When it came to music however, Dizzy Gillespie was extremely focused.

![Image 3](https://swingandbeyond.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Lorraine-002-6.jpg)Later in 1937, Gillespie met a young dancer named Lorraine Willis (1920-2004) at a theater in Washington, D.C. (probably the Howard). She worked the Afro-American Washington–Baltimore–Philadelphia–New York City theater circuit which included the the Apollo Theater in Harlem. Ms. Willis was not immediately friendly, but Dizzy pursued her nevertheless. The two eventually married in Boston on May 9, 1940, after Dizzy had become a successful and well-paid member of Cab Calloway’s band. Dizzy and Lorraine had a successful marriage, and she was always a rock of stability and support in his career and life. Lorraine became the _de facto_ personal manager of Dizzy Gillespie from the date of their marriage until Dizzy’s death in 1993.(3) _(Above left: Lorraine Willis Gillespie in the 1940s.)_

Gillespie stayed with Teddy Hill’s band for a year, then left and freelanced with other bands. In the summer of 1939, with the help of Ms. Willis, Gillespie joined Cab Calloway’s band. He recorded one of his earliest compositions, “Pickin’ the Cabbage,” with Calloway in 1940. After an altercation with Calloway in late 1941, he was fired.

![Image 4](https://swingandbeyond.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Danny-Barker-and-Dizzy-001-8.jpg)A number of versions of the story of why Dizzy Gillespie was fired by Cab Calloway have circulated over the many decades since that incident occurred. The essence of it is that Dizzy was first and foremost an excellent musician – he would not have been in the Calloway band if he wasn’t. Calloway had a fine, swinging band as the 1930s segued into the 1940s. Cab himself was a dynamic singer and stage presence, but he had slowly built his band so that by 1940, it could and did compete with the top swing bands of the day. The major instrumental soloists in the band were Chu Berry on tenor saxophone, Cozy Cole on drums, and Dizzy Gillespie on trumpet. The Calloway band was the premier Afro-American band in the nation in terms of box office drawing power, largely because of Cab’s singing and dynamic stage presence. Consequently, the sidemen with Cab were paid salaries that exceeded those paid by all other black bandleaders, and indeed most white bandleaders._(The world of swing was racially segregated, and as in all other areas that separation resulted in substantially lower salaries for black musicians than those earned by their white counterparts.)_ Whenever a musician was fortunate enough to be hired by Cab Calloway, he could count on steady work and better pay than he could receive just about anywhere else. The musicians in his band endured a lot of hard work and travel with Cab, but very few chose to leave. The money was too good. _(Above right: Dizzy in repose – 1940. Photo by Milt Hinton.)_

![Image 5](https://swingandbeyond.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Dizzy-Cab-001-001-8.jpg)Dizzy Gillespie, like any other young musician who was lucky and talented enough to get into the Calloway band, basically enjoyed the high-profile work the band did, and of course the pay, which was much greater than he had ever received before. But Dizzy was a creative musician, and he soon grew tired of the repetition that was required of various of Cab’s hits that had to be played exactly the same way nightly to satisfy Cab’s big audiences. His musical frustration was expressed by him often playing solos that the other musicians in the Calloway band (except for Chu Berry) found to be “way out.” Cab himself tolerated Gillespie’s musical adventurism because Dizzy was also an absolutely first-rate section player who could read anything, and always played his parts in the trumpet section with great accuracy. He also tolerated Dizzy’s antics onstage, which often came close to stealing the spotlight away from Cab. But after some time, Cab’s patience with Gillespie began to wear thin. I suspect that Cab took Dizzy aside and told him privately to tone-down the onstage hijinx. But as so often is the case among highly-strung performers who have been appearing before audiences together (and indeed living together) for months on end, nerves snap. Something happened onstage in front of an audience that enraged Cab. _(Above left: Dizzy Gillespie at a backstage party with fellow Calloway sidemen Keg Johnson (at rear) and Cozy Cole. Photo by Milt Hinton.)_

I will quote Cab Calloway directly, from his reminiscences some 35 years after this incident. By then, the truth had come out, and Cab recognized that he had been unfair to Dizzy by accusing him of something he hadn’t done, and then firing him. Here is what he said: _“”I fired Dizzy because of his clowning. Lord, did he clown. He would sit up there in the back row cutting-up and throwing spitballs. One night, during a performance, I was hit by two spitballs. Normally Dizzy limited his kidding to the other guys in the band, but this time, it seemed to me that he had overdone it. After the show, I was steaming. I walked into the musicians’ dressing room and confronted Dizzy. ‘You hit me with those spitballs, man. That don’t go in this band.’ ‘What!’ Dizzy said. ‘You hit me with those spitballs and you’re fired!’ ‘But I didn’t do nothin.’ ‘You’re out man.'”_ (4) Cab did not mention what happened next. Dizzy took out a knife, and he and Cab tussled. When that was over, Cab had been stabbed in the leg, and had some other minor cuts. It was a bad scene.

![Image 6](https://swingandbeyond.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Calloway-band-summer-1941-001-6.jpg)

_Cab Calloway and his band record – summer 1941. L-R: Front: Chu Berry, Andrew Brown, Hilton Jefferson (hidden behind Cab), Cab Calloway, Jerry Blake, Walter “Foots” Thomas; back: Milt Hinton, Cozy Cole, Danny Barker, Jonah Jones, Lammar Wright, Dizzy Gillespie. The two trombonists who are visible are Keg Johnson and Quentin “Butter” Jackson. Pianist Benny Payne and trombonist Tyree Glenn are not visible._

Cab then picked up the narrative: “Fifteen years later, my friend (and former long-time Calloway band bassist) Milt Hinton and I met in New York. We were having a drink and Milt said: ‘There’s something I’ve got to tell you Cab. It wasn’t Dizzy that hit you with those spitballs, _it was me._ But you were so angry I was afraid you’d fire me instead of Dizzy.'”(5)

During his time in Calloway’s band, Gillespie started writing big band arrangements that he sold to white bandleaders like Jimmy Dorsey and Charlie Barnet, among others. Post Calloway, he then freelanced as a jazz trumpeter with a number of bands including those led by Ella Fitzgerald, Benny Carter, Charlie Barnet, Les Hite, Calvin Jackson, Lucky Millinder, Earl Hines, John Kirby and Billy Eckstine. By late in 1944, _“…Gillespie’s name and the word_ bop _acquired great prominence among musicians. In early 1945, after fronting a small group at the Three Deuces in New York, Gillespie toured with his first big band. Toward the end of 1945, he formed a small combo in California. He reorganized a big band in 1946, toured Scandinavia in January and February of 1948, and broke up his big band in early 1950.”_(6)

![Image 7](https://swingandbeyond.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Bird-and-Diz-4.jpg)_“Although it has been the subject of much dispute whether Dizzy Gillespie of Charlie Parker was the primary influence in shaping the bop revolution in jazz, the truth seems to be that their ideas and those of several others were interdependent, and that each drew upon the others’ ingenuity. The result was a melodic, harmonic and rhythmic advancement of jazz (and) the incorporation of many subtleties that call for a more developed technique than had hitherto been at the disposition of most jazzmen.”_ (7) _(Above right: Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie – late 1940s.)_

On January 6, 1953 at a party Dizzy gave for his wife Lorraine at a Manhattan club called Snookie’s, during the revelry someone stepped on Dizzy’s trumpet causing the bell to be bent upward at a 45 degree angle. Dizzy liked the way this made his trumpet sound, and after that had all of his trumpets made with the bell pointed upward. It became one of many Gillespie trademarks.(7A)

**The music:**

**Dizzy Gillespie’s RCA Victor recording of “Dizzier and Dizzier” begins with an introduction that has him on open trumpet alluding to the main rather morose melody of the piece as he plays simply over sustained ensemble chords. The first chorus has Gillespie playing the unusual, rangy melody, with interesting trumpet asides. Once again, the background he plays against is thickly harmonized sustained chords. Pianist James Foreman shadows Gillespie’s solo.**

**The transition between choruses has the trombones and reeds blended, with Dizzy’s trumpet leading the ensemble into an open trombone solo possibly played by Sam Hurt. In this sequence, arranger Gerald Wilson employed the harmonized saxophone quintet to contrast with the brassy trombone sonority. After an ensemble eruption, we hear both the trombone and Gillespie’s trumpet, then Dizzy alone as he plays into the cadence and finale.**

The composer and arranger of “Dizzier and Dizzier” was Gerald Wilson, who replaced Sy Oliver in Jimmie Lunceford’s band in 1939. In the Lunceford band, Wilson worked mainly as a trumpeter, though he did write some compositions/arrangements for that band including “Hi Spook,” and “Yard Dog Mazurka,”(8) which were recorded. While leading big bands that featured his arrangements off and on from the mid-1940s through the 1960s, he gained a measure of success working as an arranger for a wide array of performers including Nancy Wilson, Julie London, Sarah Vaughan, Ray Charles and Duke Ellington.

## **“Dizzier and Dizzier”**

(aka “Katy”)

Composed and arranged by Gerald Wilson; original arrangement revised by Lew Quadling.

**Recorded by Frankie Carle and His Orchestra for Dot in 1968 in Hollywood.**

Lew Quadling directing: Frankie Carle, piano. (Probable personnel): Shorty Sherock, Cappy Lewis, Graham Young, Uan Rasey and Conte Candoli, trumpets; Dick Nash, Milt Bernhart, Lloyd Ulyate, tenor trombones; George Roberts, bass trombone; Arthur “Skeets” Herfurt, first alto saxophone, Wilbur Schwartz, alto saxophone; Georgie Auld and Gene Cipriano, tenor saxophones; Chuck Gentry, baritone saxophone; Bob Bain, guitar; Ray Brown, bass; Alvin Stoller, drums. Conte Candoli trumpet soloist; Georgie Auld, tenor saxophone soloist.

**The music:**

This performance is by an _ad hoc_ band of Hollywood sharpshooter studio musicians who play Lew Quadling’s revised version of Gerald Wilson’s arrangement with authority and panache. The titular leader of the band, swing era **veteran pianist Frankie Carle (arranger Lew Quadling was the actual leader of the musicians in the studio), plays his parts with deft accuracy. The featured trumpeter, Conte Candoli, was a Dizzy Gillespie disciple of long-standing. His playing here is a fitting homage to the Master. In place of the trombone solo in the second chorus, arranger Quadling provides a place for tenor saxophonist Georgie Auld to play a soulful solo.**

This is a creative reimagining of the original Gillespie-Wilson music that is beautifully performed and recorded.

The recordings presented with this post were digitally remastered by Mike Zirpolo.

# “Dizzier and Dizzier” (1949) Dizzy Gillespie/Gerald Wilson / (1968) Frankie Carle/Lew Quadling with Conte Candoli and Georgie Auld

![Image 1](https://swingandbeyond.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/DG-Complete-Victor-649x400.jpg)

[Video 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Fj-CWWX6Nso)

## **“Dizzier and Dizzier”**

(aka “Katy”)

Composed and arranged by Gerald Wilson.

**Recorded by Dizzy Gillespie and His Orchestra for RCA Victor on May 6, 1949 in Chicago.**

John B. “Dizzy” Gillespie, trumpet, directing: Benny Harris and Elmon Wright and Willie Cook, trumpets; Andy Duryea, Sam Hurt, Jesse Tarrant, trombones; John Brown and Ernie Henry, alto saxophones; Yusef Lateef and Joe Gayles, tenor saxophones; Al Gibson, baritone saxophone; James “Hen Gates” Foreman, piano; Al McKibbon, bass; Teddy Stewart, drums.

**The story:**

**John Birks “Dizzy” Gillespie** (1917-1993), the youngest of nine children of Lottie and James Gillespie, was born in Cheraw, South Carolina. His father was a local bandleader, so instruments were made available to the Gillespie children, including John. James died when John was only ten years old.

John Gillespie started to play the piano at age four; and by the time he was 12, he had taught himself how to play the trombone and the trumpet.

From the night in the mid-1930s Gillespie when heard trumpet wizard Roy Eldridge on the radio, he dreamed of becoming a professional musician. He won a music scholarship to the Laurinburg Institute in North Carolina, where he attended for two years, from age sixteen to eighteen. During this time, he studied harmony and theory, but not trumpet. Nevertheless, he continued developing proficiency on that instrument. He moved with his family to Philadelphia in 1935.

![Image 2](https://swingandbeyond.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Dizzy-1930s-2.jpg)Gillespie’s first job as a professional trumpeter was with Frank Fairfax’s band in 1935. Another young trumpeter was in that band then, Charlie Shavers. Gillespie, Shavers, and a bit later, Harry Edison were young musicians who advanced the technical possibilities of the trumpet in the late 1930s and into the 1940s. Stylistically, Gillespie was a follower of Roy Eldridge in the mid and late 1930s. He replaced Frankie Newton (who had previously replaced Roy Eldridge) (1) in Teddy Hill’s band in May of 1937, then he went on tour of France and England in the summer of 1937 with the Hill band. _(A link to a recording Gillespie made with Teddy Hill can be accessed at endnote 2.)_

Gillespie earned his nickname “Dizzy” while playing with the Fairfax band. It was bestowed upon him by colleagues because of his clowning, which happened both onstage and off. When it came to music however, Dizzy Gillespie was extremely focused.

![Image 3](https://swingandbeyond.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Lorraine-002-6.jpg)Later in 1937, Gillespie met a young dancer named Lorraine Willis (1920-2004) at a theater in Washington, D.C. (probably the Howard). She worked the Afro-American Washington–Baltimore–Philadelphia–New York City theater circuit which included the the Apollo Theater in Harlem. Ms. Willis was not immediately friendly, but Dizzy pursued her nevertheless. The two eventually married in Boston on May 9, 1940, after Dizzy had become a successful and well-paid member of Cab Calloway’s band. Dizzy and Lorraine had a successful marriage, and she was always a rock of stability and support in his career and life. Lorraine became the _de facto_ personal manager of Dizzy Gillespie from the date of their marriage until Dizzy’s death in 1993.(3) _(Above left: Lorraine Willis Gillespie in the 1940s.)_

Gillespie stayed with Teddy Hill’s band for a year, then left and freelanced with other bands. In the summer of 1939, with the help of Ms. Willis, Gillespie joined Cab Calloway’s band. He recorded one of his earliest compositions, “Pickin’ the Cabbage,” with Calloway in 1940. After an altercation with Calloway in late 1941, he was fired.

![Image 4](https://swingandbeyond.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Danny-Barker-and-Dizzy-001-8.jpg)A number of versions of the story of why Dizzy Gillespie was fired by Cab Calloway have circulated over the many decades since that incident occurred. The essence of it is that Dizzy was first and foremost an excellent musician – he would not have been in the Calloway band if he wasn’t. Calloway had a fine, swinging band as the 1930s segued into the 1940s. Cab himself was a dynamic singer and stage presence, but he had slowly built his band so that by 1940, it could and did compete with the top swing bands of the day. The major instrumental soloists in the band were Chu Berry on tenor saxophone, Cozy Cole on drums, and Dizzy Gillespie on trumpet. The Calloway band was the premier Afro-American band in the nation in terms of box office drawing power, largely because of Cab’s singing and dynamic stage presence. Consequently, the sidemen with Cab were paid salaries that exceeded those paid by all other black bandleaders, and indeed most white bandleaders._(The world of swing was racially segregated, and as in all other areas that separation resulted in substantially lower salaries for black musicians than those earned by their white counterparts.)_ Whenever a musician was fortunate enough to be hired by Cab Calloway, he could count on steady work and better pay than he could receive just about anywhere else. The musicians in his band endured a lot of hard work and travel with Cab, but very few chose to leave. The money was too good. _(Above right: Dizzy in repose – 1940. Photo by Milt Hinton.)_

![Image 5](https://swingandbeyond.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Dizzy-Cab-001-001-8.jpg)Dizzy Gillespie, like any other young musician who was lucky and talented enough to get into the Calloway band, basically enjoyed the high-profile work the band did, and of course the pay, which was much greater than he had ever received before. But Dizzy was a creative musician, and he soon grew tired of the repetition that was required of various of Cab’s hits that had to be played exactly the same way nightly to satisfy Cab’s big audiences. His musical frustration was expressed by him often playing solos that the other musicians in the Calloway band (except for Chu Berry) found to be “way out.” Cab himself tolerated Gillespie’s musical adventurism because Dizzy was also an absolutely first-rate section player who could read anything, and always played his parts in the trumpet section with great accuracy. He also tolerated Dizzy’s antics onstage, which often came close to stealing the spotlight away from Cab. But after some time, Cab’s patience with Gillespie began to wear thin. I suspect that Cab took Dizzy aside and told him privately to tone-down the onstage hijinx. But as so often is the case among highly-strung performers who have been appearing before audiences together (and indeed living together) for months on end, nerves snap. Something happened onstage in front of an audience that enraged Cab. _(Above left: Dizzy Gillespie at a backstage party with fellow Calloway sidemen Keg Johnson (at rear) and Cozy Cole. Photo by Milt Hinton.)_

I will quote Cab Calloway directly, from his reminiscences some 35 years after this incident. By then, the truth had come out, and Cab recognized that he had been unfair to Dizzy by accusing him of something he hadn’t done, and then firing him. Here is what he said: _“”I fired Dizzy because of his clowning. Lord, did he clown. He would sit up there in the back row cutting-up and throwing spitballs. One night, during a performance, I was hit by two spitballs. Normally Dizzy limited his kidding to the other guys in the band, but this time, it seemed to me that he had overdone it. After the show, I was steaming. I walked into the musicians’ dressing room and confronted Dizzy. ‘You hit me with those spitballs, man. That don’t go in this band.’ ‘What!’ Dizzy said. ‘You hit me with those spitballs and you’re fired!’ ‘But I didn’t do nothin.’ ‘You’re out man.'”_ (4) Cab did not mention what happened next. Dizzy took out a knife, and he and Cab tussled. When that was over, Cab had been stabbed in the leg, and had some other minor cuts. It was a bad scene.

![Image 6](https://swingandbeyond.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Calloway-band-summer-1941-001-6.jpg)

_Cab Calloway and his band record – summer 1941. L-R: Front: Chu Berry, Andrew Brown, Hilton Jefferson (hidden behind Cab), Cab Calloway, Jerry Blake, Walter “Foots” Thomas; back: Milt Hinton, Cozy Cole, Danny Barker, Jonah Jones, Lammar Wright, Dizzy Gillespie. The two trombonists who are visible are Keg Johnson and Quentin “Butter” Jackson. Pianist Benny Payne and trombonist Tyree Glenn are not visible._

Cab then picked up the narrative: “Fifteen years later, my friend (and former long-time Calloway band bassist) Milt Hinton and I met in New York. We were having a drink and Milt said: ‘There’s something I’ve got to tell you Cab. It wasn’t Dizzy that hit you with those spitballs, _it was me._ But you were so angry I was afraid you’d fire me instead of Dizzy.'”(5)

During his time in Calloway’s band, Gillespie started writing big band arrangements that he sold to white bandleaders like Jimmy Dorsey and Charlie Barnet, among others. Post Calloway, he then freelanced as a jazz trumpeter with a number of bands including those led by Ella Fitzgerald, Benny Carter, Charlie Barnet, Les Hite, Calvin Jackson, Lucky Millinder, Earl Hines, John Kirby and Billy Eckstine. By late in 1944, _“…Gillespie’s name and the word_ bop _acquired great prominence among musicians. In early 1945, after fronting a small group at the Three Deuces in New York, Gillespie toured with his first big band. Toward the end of 1945, he formed a small combo in California. He reorganized a big band in 1946, toured Scandinavia in January and February of 1948, and broke up his big band in early 1950.”_(6)

![Image 7](https://swingandbeyond.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Bird-and-Diz-4.jpg)_“Although it has been the subject of much dispute whether Dizzy Gillespie of Charlie Parker was the primary influence in shaping the bop revolution in jazz, the truth seems to be that their ideas and those of several others were interdependent, and that each drew upon the others’ ingenuity. The result was a melodic, harmonic and rhythmic advancement of jazz (and) the incorporation of many subtleties that call for a more developed technique than had hitherto been at the disposition of most jazzmen.”_ (7) _(Above right: Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie – late 1940s.)_

On January 6, 1953 at a party Dizzy gave for his wife Lorraine at a Manhattan club called Snookie’s, during the revelry someone stepped on Dizzy’s trumpet causing the bell to be bent upward at a 45 degree angle. Dizzy liked the way this made his trumpet sound, and after that had all of his trumpets made with the bell pointed upward. It became one of many Gillespie trademarks.(7A)

**The music:**

**Dizzy Gillespie’s RCA Victor recording of “Dizzier and Dizzier” begins with an introduction that has him on open trumpet alluding to the main rather morose melody of the piece as he plays simply over sustained ensemble chords. The first chorus has Gillespie playing the unusual, rangy melody, with interesting trumpet asides. Once again, the background he plays against is thickly harmonized sustained chords. Pianist James Foreman shadows Gillespie’s solo.**

**The transition between choruses has the trombones and reeds blended, with Dizzy’s trumpet leading the ensemble into an open trombone solo possibly played by Sam Hurt. In this sequence, arranger Gerald Wilson employed the harmonized saxophone quintet to contrast with the brassy trombone sonority. After an ensemble eruption, we hear both the trombone and Gillespie’s trumpet, then Dizzy alone as he plays into the cadence and finale.**

The composer and arranger of “Dizzier and Dizzier” was Gerald Wilson, who replaced Sy Oliver in Jimmie Lunceford’s band in 1939. In the Lunceford band, Wilson worked mainly as a trumpeter, though he did write some compositions/arrangements for that band including “Hi Spook,” and “Yard Dog Mazurka,”(8) which were recorded. While leading big bands that featured his arrangements off and on from the mid-1940s through the 1960s, he gained a measure of success working as an arranger for a wide array of performers including Nancy Wilson, Julie London, Sarah Vaughan, Ray Charles and Duke Ellington.

## **“Dizzier and Dizzier”**

(aka “Katy”)

Composed and arranged by Gerald Wilson; original arrangement revised by Lew Quadling.

**Recorded by Frankie Carle and His Orchestra for Dot in 1968 in Hollywood.**

Lew Quadling directing: Frankie Carle, piano. (Probable personnel): Shorty Sherock, Cappy Lewis, Graham Young, Uan Rasey and Conte Candoli, trumpets; Dick Nash, Milt Bernhart, Lloyd Ulyate, tenor trombones; George Roberts, bass trombone; Arthur “Skeets” Herfurt, first alto saxophone, Wilbur Schwartz, alto saxophone; Georgie Auld and Gene Cipriano, tenor saxophones; Chuck Gentry, baritone saxophone; Bob Bain, guitar; Ray Brown, bass; Alvin Stoller, drums. Conte Candoli trumpet soloist; Georgie Auld, tenor saxophone soloist.

**The music:**

This performance is by an _ad hoc_ band of Hollywood sharpshooter studio musicians who play Lew Quadling’s revised version of Gerald Wilson’s arrangement with authority and panache. The titular leader of the band, swing era **veteran pianist Frankie Carle (arranger Lew Quadling was the actual leader of the musicians in the studio), plays his parts with deft accuracy. The featured trumpeter, Conte Candoli, was a Dizzy Gillespie disciple of long-standing. His playing here is a fitting homage to the Master. In place of the trombone solo in the second chorus, arranger Quadling provides a place for tenor saxophonist Georgie Auld to play a soulful solo.**

This is a creative reimagining of the original Gillespie-Wilson music that is beautifully performed and recorded.

The recordings presented with this post were digitally remastered by Mike Zirpolo.

Tracks 2-7 to 2-10, 2-12, 2-13, 2-18, 2-22, and 2-23 are previously unissued.

## About This Release

So it is as appropriate as it is welcome that the latest Aleph issue focuses on Schifrin the pianist as much as Shifrin the composer. He is joined by 'Jazz Meets the Symphony' veteran, James Morrison, equally prodigious on trumpet and trombone, and tourist James Moody, who was a leading light in Dizzy Gillespie's matchless 1940's Big Band and who subsequently worked with the trumpeter on many other occasions. Schifrin is also joined by Dennis Budimir on guitar, bassist Brian Bromberg and percussionist Alex Acuna. Of the nine selections, six are Schifrin tunes. As one would expect, they testify to the rich variety of his writer's palette and range of mood; they equally enshrine the sumptuous quality of his pianism.

## About This Release

So it is as appropriate as it is welcome that the latest Aleph issue focuses on Schifrin the pianist as much as Shifrin the composer. He is joined by 'Jazz Meets the Symphony' veteran, James Morrison, equally prodigious on trumpet and trombone, and tourist James Moody, who was a leading light in Dizzy Gillespie's matchless 1940's Big Band and who subsequently worked with the trumpeter on many other occasions. Schifrin is also joined by Dennis Budimir on guitar, bassist Brian Bromberg and percussionist Alex Acuna. Of the nine selections, six are Schifrin tunes. As one would expect, they testify to the rich variety of his writer's palette and range of mood; they equally enshrine the sumptuous quality of his pianism.
